pages.x: The Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev, angry at American nuclear missiles in Turkey and wanting to protect Castro after the Bay of Pigs, secretly sent nuclear missiles to Cuba in 1962, close enough to hit most American cities within minutes.

On 14 October an American spy plane photographed missile sites being built in the Cuban countryside. President Kennedy and his advisers met in secret for a week. Some generals wanted to bomb the sites and invade. Kennedy chose a naval blockade instead, to stop more missiles arriving, and told the world on television on 22 October.

Soviet ships sailed toward the American line, and nuclear bombers were kept in the air. On 27 October an American spy plane was shot down over Cuba, and American ships dropped small depth charges on a Soviet submarine whose officers, cut off from Moscow, argued over firing a nuclear torpedo. One of them, Vasily Arkhipov, said no.

On 28 October Khrushchev agreed to take the missiles away, in return for an American promise never to invade Cuba, and a secret promise to remove the American missiles from Turkey. The world breathed again. Castro, who had not been asked, was furious.
A direct line between the White House and the Kremlin, set up in 1963 so the two leaders could talk at once in a crisis. It began as a teleprinter, not a red telephone.
pages.fx: It was the first of many steps to stop the Cold War blowing up by accident, followed that same year by a treaty banning nuclear tests in the air, in space and under the sea.

pages.x: The crisis was the closest the world has come to nuclear war. It frightened both sides into talking, and the years after it brought the first treaties to limit nuclear weapons. It is still studied as a lesson in how leaders can step back from the edge.
pts: Soviet missiles were found in Cuba
Ended when Khrushchev took them away
